title: Daodejing, chapter 1 (Mawangdui silk manuscripts)
language: Classical Chinese (silk transcription; received text) / English
source: Mawangdui Laozi A and B silk manuscripts (plates of Changsha Mawangdui Han mu jianbo jicheng vol. 1, via Wikimedia Commons) + Wikisource column transcription + Wang Bi received text (Wikisource) + Legge 1891 English (Project Gutenberg)
description: Daodejing chapter 1 as written on the two Mawangdui silk manuscripts of the Laozi (before 168 BCE), with Legge's English and the received Chinese text.
introduction:
Chapter 1 of the Daodejing (Laozi), shown on the two oldest nearly complete copies of the work: the silk manuscripts Laozi A and Laozi B, found in 1973 in Tomb 3 at Mawangdui, Changsha (Hunan), a tomb sealed in 168 BCE. Laozi A is written in a script between seal and clerical forms and does not avoid the personal name of the Han founder Liu Bang (邦); it is commonly dated before 195 BCE. Laozi B is in clerical script, avoids 邦, and is commonly dated 194-180 BCE. Both put the De part (chapters 38-81) before the Dao part (chapters 1-37), and a few chapters stand in a different order from the received text.

Each section gives the silk transcription column by column, with the Jicheng column number before each column (for Laozi B, 上 and 下 are the upper and lower halves of a column, photographed on facing plates), and links to the plate that carries those columns. □ marks a lost character; ∠, ‧ and ﹦ are marks written on the silk (﹦ repeats the character before it). Below the transcription is the received text of the Wang Bi recension, which is the text James Legge translated in 1891; the silk wording differs from it, most visibly in 恆 for received 常 (the received text avoids the name of Emperor Wen, Liu Heng), in the frequent final particle 也, and in loan characters such as 胃 for 謂.
translator_notes: English: James Legge, The Tao Teh King (Sacred Books of the East 39, 1891); Legge's paragraph numbers are kept as superscripts.
Legge translated the received text, not the silk manuscripts. Where the silk wording differs, his English follows the received text shown under the transcription.
Silk transcription: Wikisource Page transcriptions of the Jicheng plates (revisions of 18 October 2026, marked not yet proofread on Wikisource), checked against the plates for each chapter opening.

translation.original_ref: Daodejing 1; Mawangdui Laozi A (甲本) col. 93 to 94; Jicheng vol. 1 plate p. 99
translation.original_text:
93道可道也非恆道也名可名也非恆名也無名萬物之始也∠有名萬物之母也□
94恆無欲也以觀其眇∠恆有欲也以觀其所噭兩者同出異名同胃玄之有玄眾眇之□
translation.edition_text: 道可道，非常道，名可名，非常名；無名，天地之始，有名，萬物之母。故常無欲，以觀其妙，常有欲，以觀其徼；此兩者，同出而異名，同謂之玄。玄之又玄，眾妙之門。
translation.text:
1The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name.

2(Conceived of as) having no name, it is the Originator of heaven and earth; (conceived of as) having a name, it is the Mother of all things.

3Always without desire we must be found,
If its deep mystery we would sound;
But if desire always within us be,
Its outer fringe is all that we shall see.

4Under these two aspects, it is really the same; but as development takes place, it receives the different names. Together we call them the Mystery. Where the Mystery is the deepest is the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful.
translation.scan_note: Laozi A (甲本), columns 93 to 94, on plate p. 99 of Changsha Mawangdui Han mu jianbo jicheng, vol. 1 (column numbers are printed under each plate; the columns run from right to left). Checked on the image: column 93 reads 道可道也非恆道也名可名也 (the opening of this chapter, with the end of the preceding text where shown). The Dao part of the manuscript begins here, after chapter 79, which closes the De part. □ marks a character lost on the silk (2 in this section). Transcription and column numbers: Wikisource 老子 (帛書甲本), which follows the Jicheng column numbering. The English is Legge's translation of the received text, shown below the silk transcription; the silk wording differs from it in many places, so compare the two Chinese texts for the variants.
